details:
**Fear and Trembling**
Kierkegaard's 1843 book on Abraham's near-sacrifice of his son Isaac, written under the pseudonym Johannes de Silentio. It is the most common title clue for him. After an opening "Panegyric upon Abraham" and a "Preliminary Expectoration," the book poses three "Problemata," including whether there is an absolute duty to God.

**"Knight of faith" vs. "knight of infinite resignation"**
The central contrast in Fear and Trembling. The knight of infinite resignation gives up what he loves, illustrated by a young man who falls in love with an unattainable princess and renounces her. The knight of faith, exemplified by Abraham, gives it up and yet believes "by virtue of the absurd" that he will get it all back.

**"Teleological suspension of the ethical"**
The question "Is there a teleological suspension of the ethical?" is Problema I of Fear and Trembling. Kierkegaard asks whether Abraham's duty to God can override universal ethics, letting the individual stand "above the universal," unlike Agamemnon, a "tragic hero" whose sacrifice of Iphigenia at Aulis stays within the ethical.

**Either/Or**
Kierkegaard's 1843 debut work, "edited" by the pseudonym Victor Eremita, which contrasts the aesthetic and ethical ways of life. The first half contains the papers of the aesthete "A," including the essay "Crop Rotation," an essay on the erotic in music, and lectures to the Symparanekromenoi (a "fellowship of the dead"). The second half is made up of letters from the ethical Judge William (Vilhelm) to "A."

**"The Seducer's Diary" and Regine Olsen**
The closing section of the first part of Either/Or, in which Johannes the seducer courts the young Cordelia and then abandons her. It mirrors Kierkegaard's own broken engagement to Regine Olsen.

**Pseudonyms**
Kierkegaard wrote many works under pseudonyms as a form of "indirect communication," to separate himself from the views expressed. They include Johannes de Silentio, Victor Eremita, Constantin Constantius, Johannes Climacus, Anti-Climacus, Vigilius Haufniensis, and Hilarius Bookbinder.

**Three stages of existence: aesthetic, ethical, religious**
Kierkegaard's progression of the "stages on life's way," from a life of pleasure, to a life of duty, to a life of faith before God. They are developed in Either/Or and in Stages on Life's Way, which is "edited" by the pseudonym Hilarius Bookbinder.

**The Sickness Unto Death**
Kierkegaard's 1849 work on despair, written under the pseudonym Anti-Climacus. It defines the self as "a relation which relates itself to itself," treats despair as sin, a failure to rest in God, and describes forms of despair that come from failing to reconcile the finite and the infinite.

**"Subjectivity is truth"**
Kierkegaard's famous claim from Concluding Unscientific Postscript to Philosophical Fragments, written as Johannes Climacus. It holds that the "subjective thinker," whose first and last trait is passion, reaches truth through a personal commitment rather than objective, systematic reasoning.

**Philosophical Fragments**
An 1844 work written as Johannes Climacus. It contrasts the Socratic "doctrine of recollection," in which truth is already inside the learner, with the Christian view that truth must come from a divine teacher, the God who appears in time.

**Repetition**
An 1843 work by the pseudonym Constantin Constantius. A "Young Man" agonizes over his engagement, and the book contrasts those who live in hope with those who live in memory, and recollection with repetition.

**The leap of faith**
Kierkegaard's idea that reason cannot bring a person to religious belief. Faith instead requires a passionate, irrational "leap" that overcomes doubt while still acknowledging it.

**The Concept of Anxiety and the "dizziness of freedom"**
An 1844 work written as Vigilius Haufniensis. It describes anxiety as "the dizziness of freedom" that a person feels when facing their own possibilities, and it connects anxiety to original sin.

**The Corsair affair**
Kierkegaard's public feud with the Copenhagen satirical newspaper The Corsair, which ridiculed him after he provoked it in an exchange connected to criticism of Stages on Life's Way. His pieces in the feud include "The Dialectical Result of a Literary Police Action."

**The Concept of Irony and opposition to Hegel**
The Concept of Irony, with Continual Reference to Socrates, was Kierkegaard's university thesis. It defines irony as "infinite absolute negativity" and compares Socrates to Christ. Throughout his career Kierkegaard parodied Hegel's philosophical system, and he later attacked the Danish state church.
